description: Issue 476 — checked-in inputs for the scoring goldens. A realistic 10-minute woodworking-channel video with 6 candidates (5 signal-origin, 1 llm-origin). scripts/record_scoring_goldens.py feeds these through the REAL score_candidates call path; tests/test_scoring_goldens.py replays the recorded responses over the same inputs.
dna_brief:
CHANNEL: WorkshopWes — practical woodworking for apartment makers.

AUDIENCE: Beginners and renters working out of small spaces with hand tools and a single cordless drill. They watch for confidence, not spectacle: the best-performing uploads show a mistake happening and the calm recovery from it.

PROVEN STYLE (from this channel's own analytics):
- Top retention spikes land on 'reveal after doubt' beats: Wes predicts a joint will fail, tests it, and reacts honestly to the result. The 3 highest-retention Shorts all open with the doubt sentence, not the test itself.
- Talking-head explanation segments longer than 20 seconds lose 30-40% of viewers; explanations that happen WHILE cutting hold retention flat.
- The audience rewards self-deprecating honesty ('I measured this wrong twice') — comment sentiment and re-watch both peak on those beats.
- Tool-review tangents and sponsor-adjacent talk underperform badly on this channel: median retention on gear talk is 45% below the channel median.
- Native Shorts length for this channel: 28-45 seconds. Clips beyond 50 seconds see swipe-away cliffs regardless of content.

WHAT TO LOOK FOR IN CLIPS: a complete setup (the doubt or the claim) followed by the test and the honest reaction, kept inside one idea. Avoid windows that open mid-explanation or that end before the result lands.

candidates.llm_reason: Wes admits he measured the shelf twice and got two different numbers — a self-deprecating honesty beat with a complete setup and payoff inside the window.

transcript_segments.text: Welcome back to the workshop. Today we are building a floating shelf with zero visible screws.
Everything here gets done with a pull saw, a chisel, and one cordless drill.
First step is ripping this pine board down to width.
If your saw wanders like mine does, clamp a guide block right on the line.
That is the whole trick. Cheap board, straight cut.
Let the glue set for a minute.
Okay. Now the part I have been dreading.
The hidden bracket has to sit perfectly level or the whole shelf tips forward.
I marked the studs earlier, so let us get this on the wall.
Driving the first lag bolt in now.
Second bolt. Snug, not crushed.
Here is the thing about these dowel joints though.
Everyone online says glued dowels can hold eighty pounds. I genuinely do not believe that.
So I loaded this test piece with every clamp I own. That is about ninety pounds of cast iron.
It held. It actually held! I am a little offended, honestly.
So yes, the internet wins this round. Dowels are stronger than my pride.
Which means the shelf design does not need metal brackets at all.
Let me clean up this glue squeeze-out before it dries.
A damp rag now saves you twenty minutes of sanding later.
Right, next board.
While this clamps up, quick word about measuring.
I measured this shelf opening twice and got two different numbers. Twice!
Turns out my tape measure hook is bent, so every inside measurement was an eighth off.
Check your hook against a ruler. Mine has been lying to me for a year.
The fix cost nothing: I just burned an inch and measured from the one mark.
Old carpenter trick, still undefeated.
Now for the chisel work on the bracket mortise.
Take shallow passes. The chisel should whisper, not bite.
This mortise is where I ruined the last two attempts at this design.
If the walls are not square the bracket rocks, and a rocking bracket means a sagging shelf.
Moment of truth. Sliding the shelf onto the bracket.
Dead level. First try this time. That has never happened on this channel.
Three failed prototypes taught me more than any tutorial did.
The sanding progression is 120 then 180 then a hand block at 220.
Do not skip grits. Skipping grits is how you get those swirl marks.
Wipe-on poly, thin coats.
So my neighbor walks in while the finish is drying.
He puts his coffee mug on the wet shelf. The WET shelf. The one with the sign on it.
There is now a perfect mug ring in my finish and honestly, I cannot even be mad.
We are calling it a design feature. A built-in coaster memorial.
One more coat fixes it. Nothing in woodworking is ever really ruined.
Quick recap of the budget for anyone keeping score.
Board was twelve dollars, dowels were three, finish I already had.
Fifteen dollars for a shelf that holds ninety pounds with no visible hardware.
If you build one, tag me. I read everything.
Next week we are building the matching bracket-free bookend. See you then.
